title: GitHub Beyond Coding: The Agentic Engineering Loop

shape.slideLayout: 3 section dividers + 11 scene presentation cards + 1 closing takeaway
shape.sentence: A nine-concern engineering graph shown in eleven demo scenes; only one concern is coding.
shape.note: This is a graph, not a queue. Work enters at more than one concern and travels along more than one edge. The left-to-right reading below is one path through the graph, chosen because it is easy to narrate, and it is never the definition of the system. Scenes are how the hour is presented; concerns are what the graph is made of. Never conflate the two counts.

concerns.name: Signal
concerns.question: What changed or deserves attention?
concerns.primitive: Scheduled, bounded automation that reads committed evidence and proposes work

concerns.name: Intent
concerns.question: Why should we act?
concerns.primitive: Durable, assignable work items an agent can read where the code lives

concerns.name: Contract
concerns.question: What must remain true?
concerns.primitive: A specification, a decision record and acceptance criteria stored beside the code

concerns.name: Lane
concerns.question: Who or what should act?
concerns.primitive: Interchangeable execution surfaces bound by one repository contract

concerns.name: Implementation
concerns.question: What changed?
concerns.primitive: A reviewable change set with line-level discussion

concerns.name: Evidence
concerns.question: Does it work and remain secure?
concerns.primitive: Deterministic checks and security scanning bound to that change set

concerns.name: Authority
concerns.question: Who accepts the risk?
concerns.primitive: Required review by named owners, attributed to a person on a commit

concerns.name: Release
concerns.question: What is allowed to ship?
concerns.primitive: Environment approval, federated credentials, build provenance

concerns.name: Production
concerns.question: What happened after release?
concerns.primitive: A path for production signal to re-enter the graph as work

entryPoints.label: Telemetry
entryPoints.example: A scheduled workflow reads committed telemetry and finds a rate that moved. This hour enters here.

entryPoints.label: Business intent
entryPoints.example: Somebody opens an issue because the business wants an outcome. Nothing had to change first.

entryPoints.label: Security finding
entryPoints.example: A scanner raises an alert about code that already merged, and the graph runs backwards from evidence.

entryPoints.label: Production incident
entryPoints.example: A release misbehaves, and the observation is the first thing anyone writes down.

feedbackEdges.note: A failing check either found a defect in the change or a defect in what the contract asked for.
A reviewer who declines is rarely rejecting the code. Usually the intent or the constraint was wrong.
Production may raise a new signal, reshape intent, change what must remain true, or open a proposal directly.

concernMapping.$comment: Every scene declares which concern it puts on the screen. A scene marked crossCutting frames the graph rather than demonstrating one concern of it, and does not count towards coverage: each of the nine canonical concerns must be demonstrated by at least one scene that is not cross-cutting. sceneMarker is what the card subtitle and the presenter crosswalk both render, so the two can never drift.

scenes.tabRouting: Stay on tab 1 for the whole scene.
scenes.title: The hard part is not writing code. It is steering change.
scenes.expectedState: The engineering graph: nine concerns, four entry points, and the feedback edges that run backwards. Implementation is the only coding concern.
scenes.stopCondition: If the deck will not enter slides mode, present the article view and continue.
scenes.question: Nine concerns, nine questions
scenes.sceneMarker: The whole graph · Nine concerns, nine questions

scenes.tabRouting: Open tab 3 first for the finished issue, then tab 2 for the source and the run.
scenes.title: Work can enter from anywhere; make the next step durable.
scenes.expectedState: The four entry points first, then the finished issue on screen within fifteen seconds, then the pipeline and the bounded control contract in the frontmatter. A fresh run is triggered into the background only.
scenes.stopCondition: Show the finished issue first, always. Never make the room watch a queue.

trustModel.note: The input is committed synthetic telemetry: reviewed repository content, not attacker-controlled. The control that matters here is the bounded, code-reviewable contract in the frontmatter, not an input gate.

scenes.question: What changed or deserves attention?
scenes.sceneMarker: Signal · What changed or deserves attention?

scenes.tabRouting: Stay on tab 3; scroll to the intake comment.
scenes.title: Turn noise into intent before asking an agent to code.
scenes.expectedState: Prepared output: one triage comment with four headings and at most three allowlisted labels, and the safe next action it names.
scenes.stopCondition: Three minutes, hard. Prepared only: the OpenCode lock reports the firewall disabled and maps the Copilot token into the model sandbox. Never run this lane live.

trustModel.note: Issue text is attacker-controlled. This lane is the one that needs the label and actor gate, and it has one; the pulse lane does not need it because its input is committed content.
